supporting_evidence.text:
Occasioned by the death of Creveliers oﬀ Astypalaia:
The island’s role in the raids by Catholic corsairs during the 17th century
Giorgos Koutzakiotis
Between shortly before midnight of the 24th and early morning of the 25th of September 1679, the life of
French corsair Hugues Creveliers, leader of the most important corsair company active in the Aegean sea
in the 1670s, came to an inglorious end oﬀ the coast of Astypalaia, due to the blowing up of his ship by a
member of his crew. The present study takes a closer look at the details of the event and attempts to
portray the role that Astypalaia played in the raids of Catholic privateers against the Ottomans during the
seventeenth century; raids which had become a regular occurrence because of the protracted VenetianOttoman wars. The privileged geographical location of the island made it an ideal base for the corsairs to
launch their attacks against commercial ships following the routes between Alexandria and Constantinople.
At the same time, Astypalaia was an excellent hideout for corsairs, not only because they could ﬁnd provisions there (such as bread, wine, etc.) and stock up with drinking water, but also because the island provided
plenty of safe anchorages. The names of Astypalaia’s havens in French and Italian portolan texts, along with
other information of the time (testimonies about corsair contracts written on the island and marriages
between privateers and local Greek women), attest not only the strong relationship that the corsairs built
with Astypalaia, but also the degree of appropriation of the place by them. In the last part of this study we
examine the role of the bay of Vathy in the corsair raids, since this is most likely where the explosion
of Creveliers’ ship took place. This particular bay has similar traits to other anchorages in the Cycladic
islands where we know that corsairs repaired their ships, since they had built small forts or batteries at the
narrow entrances to these lairs so that no enemy ship could approach. In-situ research conducted by the
author on the south side of the narrow straits of Vathy bay led to the discovery of similar built structures
which seem to be relevant to the frequent corsair presence there.

Captain Spratt in the 1860s describes the presence of guard posts or look-outs “upon the most conspicuous
eminences along the whole coast of Crete, at distances of eight or ten miles apart, whose beacon-fires blaze up at

1865, 3). A similar system was recently described by Andrew Blackler (2022) and a series of soroi, beacons or
pyres, have been identified in the Pediada of Crete. These could have been used for signaling and alerting in case
of attacks (Sarris et al. 2011; Panagiotaki et al. 2020). Steven Soetens (2005, 44) too has noted the similarities
between the various lookouts as shown on a Venetian map (Fig. 4) drawn by Nicola Gualdo de Priorati in 1633
and the location of peak sanctuaries (Arakadaki 1997). Could these, besides their ritual functions, also have
represented an early warning system, protecting the Cretan coasts during the heydays of Minoan civilization?
A combination of evenly spaced coastal settlements, peak sanctuaries with large vistas and beacons that could
be used in a way that tradition suggests the fall of Troy was announced would have represented a considerable
“AWACS”.
And then there is the question of pirate attacks of coastal settlements – as I said they don’t leave their
­signature and thus it is difficult to blame pirates rather than another adversary for the destruction and pillaging
of a settlement. A much-cited example is the Late Cycladic (LC) IIIC site of Koukounaries on Paros. Because
of the discovery of bodies within the destruction layer, its excavator, Dimitrios Schilardi (1979; 1984), blamed
pirates, but apparently the site was not pillaged, which would be strange in case of a pirate attack (Vlachopoulos
2003). Each site in fact should be explored in detail: How did the destruction happen? Was it partial or ­complete?

so that it could be pillaged again. Bergen in Norway, for example, was pillaged by pirates in 1428, 1429 and 1432

Plutarch and Polyaenus refer to the pirates who captured Julius Caesar as Cilicians, while the other sources
do not specify their identity. Therefore, it cannot be certain whether the pirates were Cilicians, Milesians or
whether a mixed band − a fairly common occurrence in pirate crews. Perhaps, there was confusion between
the terms Cilicians and pirates (App. Mith. 14.92) or perhaps the pirates presented themselves as coming from
a distant homeland (e.g., Cilicia), to hide their real identity and to protect (nearby) homeland from reprisals, or perhaps the relevant sources, which are all considerably later than the event, wanted to attribute the
incident to some unknown or foreign pirates. Indeed, after the final defeat of Mithridates and the end of the
­Mithridatic wars, cities like Miletus ceased trying to strike a balance between the two conflicting powers (Rome
and ­Mithridates) and sided, willingly or unwillingly, with Rome (see Kleiner 1968, 19; Sarantidis 2020, 55−6;
Cicero (Verr. 2.1.89), likewise, refers to the imposition of taxes “by the Roman people” and the participation of
Miletus in the expulsion of the pirates).
In any event, whether the pirates had Pharmakoussa as their base or were operating outside of it, or
whether they happened to locate themselves in the vicinity only once, it is difficult to accept the idea that they
went ­unnoticed by a passing ship or by guard troops, given the presence of defensive forts and watchtowers
throughout the Milesian seaboard territories, including those on Pharmakoussa itself (for the supervision of
these islands, see Sarantidis 2020, 203–23, figs. 112–21). Moreover, both the undisturbed visit of a large group of
men anchored in an island cove for thirty-eight days, and the fact that Julius Caesar himself, after he redeemed
himself and assembled a fleet, returned to the island to find the pirates still situated at the same place, would
seem to indicate that the pirates in question were able to reside on these islands (or, at least, on Pharmakoussa)
and conduct their activities unhindered during this period.
However, pirate activity in this islandscape was not limited to antiquity; in fact, pirates continued to operate
there in modern times. The Englishman Anthony Roberts, a pirate who was himself taken hostage by pirates in
1692, describes the seasonal but systematic use of the region by pirates, stating that after wintering on islands,
such as Paros, Antiparos, Ios and Melos, pirates would sail to Phournoi in early March: “And then they go for the
Furnoes [Phournoi], and lie there under the high land hid, having a watch on the hill with a little flag, whereby
they make a signal, if they see any sail; they flip out, and lie athwart the boak of Samos, and take their prize;
they lie in the same nature under Necaria [Ikaria], and Gadronise [Gaidouronisi], and Leppiso [Leipsoi] in
the spring and forepart of the summer” (Hacke 1699, 8; see also Koutsouflakis, this volume; Koutzakiotis, this

a pirate site in the following century (see Krantonelli 1998, 110, 179).

SURVEY EVIDENCE IN WESTERN ROUGH CILICIA
What the evidence of the RCSP survey has revealed is that a Hellenistic horizon of ceramic remains is ­consistent
throughout the region, but the numbers are minimal in quantity and indicate a shallow pattern of small, d
­ ispersed
settlements. As the published context ceramics of the survey indicate (Autret et al. 2019), counts of H
­ ellenistic
ceramics in the survey region were limited (6%, or 339 out of some 5418 dated sherds). It is not so much their
numbers as it is their distribution that seems significant. Hellenistic ceramics were encountered in every region
that has been investigated, including the coastal sites and ridges investigated in 1996–1999, the Adanda Canyon
in the mesogeia investigated in 2000–2003 and the highland sites in the upper Bickici river basin investigated in
2003–2011. One highland site, Sugözü Yayla (RC 1102), seems particularly noteworthy, because it sits at 1600 m
elevation, overlooking the pass that connects the Bickici River on the coast to the southern branch of the Göksu
or Calycadnus River on the interior. Moreover, Hellenistic ceramics were encountered at every categorized
locus, regardless of scale, from the large urban sites such as Iotape and Selinus, to village scale settlements, to
isolated farmsteads, kiln sites and press complexes, to random rural survey units. As we have noted previously,
the presence of pre-Roman ceramics at Iotape and Antiochia ad Cragum (Fig. 3) seems particularly important,
because both communities were established in the mid-1st century CE by the Roman client king Antiochus
IV of Commagene. What the pre-Roman pottery indicates, therefore, is that local settlements preceded these
foundations, settlements that may possibly have served as pirate bases.

act of plunder (koursos/kourson), attested as early as the 8th century (Sophocles 1888, s.v. κοῦρσον 687; ­Kriaras

Latin cursus; Heinz 2007, s.v. cursarius, cursus). The pronounced similarity between the ­numerous versions of

has fostered a conjectural association in popular consciousness, often leading to the belief that the islands derive
their name from pirate activity. This somewhat arbitrary popular perception, however, does not preclude the
historical possibility that the archipelago of Phournoi was indeed a hub of intense pirate activity in the past.
A series of coastal toponyms documented on maps or utilized in the modern vernacular of Phournoi
are probably the living remnants of pirate activity in the past: Kourniachto (a place for hiding or lurking),

Rome responded to the piracy threat by enacting the Gabinian Law in 67 BCE, granting extraordinary
powers to the outgoing consul Gnaeus Pompey to eradicate piracy throughout the Mediterranean. Pompey’s
campaign, meticulously planned and brief, relied heavily on diplomacy rather than outright armed conflict and
proved highly effective.
Unlike Pharmakoussa, which gained notoriety due to a prominent incident, Phournoi never attracted
­significant attention from ancient historians. To uncover tangible evidence of pirate activity in Phournoi, one
must turn to the late Byzantine and post-Byzantine periods.
The earliest account mentioning Phournoi as an ambush site for Turkish pirates targeting merchant vessels
comes from the Florentine monk Cristoforo Buondelmonti in the early 15th century, who was shipwrecked
on the island and endured five days without food before being rescued by a passing ship (Buondelmonti 1897,
109–10 no. 55). Buondelmonti also noted the favorable anchorages provided by Phournoi, where ships could
seek shelter at night to avoid strong winds. However, he observed the island as deserted and abandoned by its
inhabitants. Apparently, its use by Turkish pirates was seasonal, a pattern recurring over the centuries.
Historical records indicate that during the latter half of the 15th century, the Genoese administration
­ rchestrated a mass relocation of the population of Samos to Chios, primarily due to piracy thriving in neigho
boring islands and Phournoi (Hasluck 1910–1911, 169; Melas 1957, 158–59). Ottoman admiral Piri Reis also
depicted a similar scene of desolation at the beginning of the 16th century (Bülent 2002, 157). The abandonment described by Buondelmonti and Piri Reis seemingly rendered Phournoi an ideal refuge for various bands
of pirates to regroup and distribute their plunder.
In the summer of 1602, the Spanish pirate Alonso de Contreras sought refuge on the deserted islands
of Phournoi with his Maltese frigate and companions, following a series of successful operations in Serifos,
­Astypalaia, Amorgos and Patmos, intending to regroup and divide their spoils. However, they were compelled
to abandon the islands when two galleys under Suleiman of Catania, then Bey of Chios, appeared, forcing de
Contreras to flee via Ikaria and Mykonos (Durant 1975, 146–56; Krantonelli 1991, 107–9, 333; de Contreras
1994, 97–102).
The involvement of corsairs from the Order of the Knights of St. John of Malta and other Christian forces in
the Archipelago of Phournoi is corroborated by the description of Ikaria by Joseph Georgirenes, the archbishop
of Samos and Ikaria, published in London in 1677, reflecting his experiences in the early 1670s (Georgirenes
1677, 3–4, 55; Papalas 2002, 258–67). Georgirenes notes the uninhabited islets of Phournoi, located three miles
south of the coast of Ikaria, boasting natural harbors capable of accommodating various vessels. He further
mentions that at other times, corsairs from Malta and other Christian factions would lie in wait on these islands,
ambushing ships trading between Chios and Rhodes.
The daily routine of these corsair groups is vividly described by the English captive Mr. Roberts, who was
shipwrecked in Ios in 1692 and subsequently captured by pirates, forced to serve as a gunner on their ship.
­According to Roberts, the corsairs would spend the winter in Paros, Antiparos, Melos and Ios until early March.
They would then relocate to Phournoi, where they would lie in wait from early spring to mid-summer, with
lookouts stationed in the mountains overlooking the Samos-Ikaria strait, keeping watch for passing ships. They
would also venture into the southern part of Ikaria, Gaidouronisi and Leipsoi, before moving further south to
posts in Asia Minor, spanning from Cilicia to Cyprus. In autumn, they would return to the Aegean to sell their
plunder and deliver profits to their backers in Livorno, Malta or Marseille (Hacke 1699; Ormerod 1924, 17–8;
Krantonelli 1991, 89–93; Simopoulos 1994, 106).
This cyclic movement of ambush, aligned with the routes of convoys between Alexandria and C
­ onstantinople
or guided by intelligence from captured vessels, was undoubtedly a prevalent method of piracy during this era.

MAINTENANCE OF THE PIRATE AND CORSAIR SHIPS
As already pointed out, pirate and corsair operations were interrupted from time to time to cater for the
­maintenance and supply needs of the ships. The success of the operations, after all, heavily depended on the
speed of sailing, which could only be ensured by regular maintenance of the keel, scraping it clean from marine
organisms and coating it with a mixture of grease and tar. These particular jobs, namely careening and graving,
were carried out at least twice a year. Another job that took place at regular but less frequent intervals was
caulking, namely the sealing of the hull with a tar-soaked oakum.
In order to complete all these maintenance operations, the ship had to be disarmed in a suitable cove (Jal
1848, 388–89, 423, 655–56; Jurien de La Gravière 1885, 219–20; Fennis 1995, 454, 491–92, 849–50). In the case
of pirates and corsairs, the cove in question had to fulfill a number of conditions in order to be considered
suitable. First, it had to allow the ship to approach the shore as far as possible; then, it had to be secluded, and,
finally, it had to provide opportunities for defense during the works, which we shall discuss below. The German
scholar Johann Michael Wansleben, who traveled in the Ottoman territories in the 1670s, notes in one of his
manuscripts that the corsairs graved their ships during the winter months in Astypalaia and Ios, while in June
and July in Porto Chevalier (Fethiye or Şövalye Adası) and one other anchorage on the coast of Lycia (BNF, MS
NAF 4193, f. 195v).1 Other sources, however, attest that the corsairs maintained their ships on Ios, Melos (­ Gazette
1668, 650, 660; Argenti 1954, 152) and evidently on other islands even during the summer months. I­ n­deed, a
text containing comments on maps of the Archipelago informs us that sometimes the corsairs careened their
ships at Arkioi (ANF, Marine, 3JJ 221, no. 4), in the wider area of which, as we have already ­mentioned, they lay
in wait to ambush passing ships from spring until early summer.
1 I am grateful to my colleague Alastair Hamilton for pointing out this unpublished note by J.M. Wansleben.

The abovementioned bays are characterized by either a narrow entrance or one blocked by an islet, which
allowed the placement of cannons at the edges of the bay and/or on the islet to prevent enemy ships from
­approaching during maintenance work. This was a common defensive practice that was not only followed by the
Catholic corsairs. For example, in 1681, it is reported that, when corsairs from Tripoli in Libya were informed
that a French squadron was pursuing them and intended to attack them in Chios, they made plans to take refuge
in Nea Phocaea (Yenifoça), in order to maintain their ships and place cannons at the entrance of its harbor
(Argenti 1954, 164, 166, 175). What interests us here, however, is not the practice per se, but the construction of
defensive works for the placement of cannons in sites frequented by corsairs. Indeed, French portolans inform
us that, in the gulf of Melos, at the cape of Patrikia, the corsairs had constructed “a fort” (un fort) or, at least,
“something like a fort” (comme une espèce de fort) to install their cannons (ANF, Marine, 3JJ 219, no. 5, 22 and
no. 8, 49). Roberts also attests that in the gulf of Naoussa, right on the bay of Ayioi Anargyroi, the corsairs had
constructed “a small battery” for the same purpose (Hacke 1699, 47).

supporting_evidence.text:
LOOKOUTS
Beyond the installation of cannons in the bays, where the corsairs found refuge for the maintenance of their
ships, another practice, which may have left its traces in the landscape of the Archipelago, is the lookouts they
placed on the highest points around the bays they used, either as ambush points or shipyards (Earle 2010, 158).
In the 17th century, this practice is attested in Ios (Gazette 1668, 652–53; Argenti 1954, 152), in Pharmakonissi
(de Contreras 1977, 67), and, of course, in Phournoi (Hacke 1699, 8), where even today the names of the island’s
bays indicate that they were once the lairs of famous corsairs: Pano and Kato Maneta bays and, possibly, Pavlos
bay (Fig. 9).
The sentries alerted the corsairs to the appearance of ships in the distance by hoisting or waving small flags,
thus giving orders to prepare for defensive or raiding operations. This practice should probably be associated
with the name Bandieres (or Padieres) of the hill on the south side of the bay of Vathy, as the present-day
­inhabitants of Astypalaia do not have any explanation for this place name (Fig. 2). Thus, the name of the hill is
probably not related to the relatively recent Italian occupation of the island, but to the practices of sailors of an
earlier time (Koutzakiotis 2023, 231–32).
Moreover, it is no coincidence that a similar place name is found in the narrow strait between Antiparos and
Paros, where corsair ships frequently anchored. More specifically, the southernmost islet of the strait is called
Pandieronissi and, as it is the largest of a cluster of islets and skerries, it lends its name to the entire cluster:
Pandieronissia (Fig. 1). It must be added here that one of the Pandieronissia bears the name Preza (Skandalidis
2001, 185), which in the lingua franca of the time denoted the spoils of corsairs or pirates, their “prize”. “Preza”
as a micro-toponym is also encountered today in Kimolos (Katsouros 1975, 326).
